claim: Deep learning vision models that use data augmentation techniques that make non-geometric pixel-level manipulations (e.g., PixMix, AugMix) during training are robust to poisoning attacks with global triggers (e.g., manipulation of size > 95% of total image area - noise patterns, intensity/contrast manipulation) when up to 1% of the training data is poisoned.  A model is considered robust if the post-training attack success rate remains within 5% of a similar model trained using the same augmentation techniques but with only clean data.
subclaims: Do deep learning vision models using data augmentation techniques with non-geometric pixel-level manipulations during training remain robust to poisoning attacks with global triggers?
Are PixMix and AugMix examples of data augmentation techniques that make non-geometric pixel-level manipulations?
What types of global triggers are involved in the poisoning attacks?
Do the global triggers include manipulations affecting more than 95% of the total image area?
What maximum percentage of the training data is poisoned?
How is robustness defined for the model after training?
baseline_experiments: To address subclaim 1, run a controlled backdoor-poisoning benchmark on a public image dataset such as CIFAR-10 or Tiny-ImageNet from HuggingFace/Kaggle. Train the same architecture, e.g. ResNet-18 or WideResNet-28-10, under three training regimes: standard augmentation, AugMix, and PixMix. For each regime, create a poisoned training set by modifying 1% of the training images with a global trigger and changing their labels to a fixed target class, then train from scratch using identical hyperparameters and seeds. Evaluate clean accuracy and attack success rate on a triggered test set, and compare the attack success rate of the poisoned AugMix/PixMix models to the corresponding clean-data AugMix/PixMix baseline evaluated with the same trigger at test time. Robustness is supported if the poisoned model’s attack success rate is no more than 5 percentage points above the clean-data baseline; it is weakened if the increase is larger or if results are unstable across seeds. This experiment could be made less necessary by prior peer-reviewed experiments using the same dataset, architecture, trigger area, poisoning fraction, and robustness definition.

To address subclaims 3 and 4, construct and validate several global triggers before or during the main poisoning experiment: additive random noise over the full image, multiplicative intensity scaling over the full image, contrast manipulation over the full image, and a large spatial mask covering at least 95% of pixels. Use CIFAR-10 or Tiny-ImageNet and explicitly log the fraction of modified pixels for each trigger, ensuring the trigger affects more than 95% of total image area while preserving image dimensions and labels before poisoning. Then repeat the 1% poisoning protocol for each trigger type with AugMix and PixMix training, measuring whether robustness holds uniformly or only for some global triggers. If all trigger types yield attack success rates within 5 percentage points of the clean baseline, the claim is strengthened for the listed trigger classes; if only some do, the claim should be narrowed to those triggers. This experiment could be made unnecessary if the claim provider supplies exact trigger-generation code and measurements showing that the triggers modify more than 95% of pixels.

To address subclaims 2, 5, and 6, perform an implementation audit and ablation study using public AugMix and PixMix implementations. First, verify from the augmentation pipelines that AugMix and PixMix include non-geometric pixel-level manipulations such as color, contrast, brightness, posterization, solarization, noise, or mixing with procedurally generated/fractal images, rather than relying only on geometric transforms. Then train AugMix and PixMix models under poisoning rates of 0%, 0.25%, 0.5%, and 1% using the same global trigger and target-label attack, and compute the robustness criterion as: attack success rate of poisoned model minus attack success rate of the clean-data counterpart trained with the same augmentation. If robustness holds up to 1% but fails above or near 1%, the maximum-poisoning portion of the claim is supported but boundary-sensitive; if it fails below 1%, the claim is not feasible as stated. This experiment could be skipped or reduced if authoritative documentation and reproducible training logs already establish the exact augmentation operations, poisoning percentages, and robustness metric used.
method_experiments: To address subclaim 1, train identical ResNet-18 or WideResNet models on public CIFAR-10 using three training pipelines: standard crop/flip only, AugMix, and PixMix. For each augmentation pipeline, create poisoned training sets by selecting 1% of training images from non-target classes, applying global triggers covering the full image, and relabeling them to a fixed target class. Use several global triggers named in the claim: additive low-amplitude noise pattern, blended random texture, global brightness shift, and global contrast manipulation. Train at least 3 random seeds per condition. Evaluate clean accuracy and attack success rate by applying the same trigger to all non-target test images and measuring the fraction classified as the target class. Compare each poisoned AugMix/PixMix model’s ASR to the ASR of the corresponding clean-data AugMix/PixMix model; the claim is supported only if the increase is no more than 5 percentage points for all tested global triggers while clean accuracy remains comparable. If ASR rises by much more than 5 points for any trigger, the robustness claim is weakened or falsified for that setting. If standard augmentation fails but AugMix/PixMix remain within the 5-point threshold, this supports the specific value of non-geometric pixel-level augmentation. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by prior peer-reviewed results using the same datasets, triggers, poison rate, augmentation implementations, and ASR definition.

To address subclaims 3, 4, and 5, run a controlled sweep on CIFAR-10 and a second public dataset such as GTSRB or Tiny-ImageNet to test whether the claimed robustness holds specifically for global triggers affecting more than 95% of the image area and for poison rates up to 1%. Using the best-performing setup from Experiment 1, vary trigger coverage at 50%, 80%, 95%, 98%, and 100% of image area, and vary poison rate at 0%, 0.1%, 0.5%, 1%, and 2%. Use the same target-label poisoning protocol and evaluate ASR against the corresponding clean-data AugMix/PixMix baseline. Results would show whether robustness is genuinely tied to global triggers above the 95% area threshold and whether there is a sharp degradation at or below 1% poisoning. If ASR remains within 5 points for all poison rates up to 1% and all coverages above 95%, but fails at 2%, the quantitative claim is strongly supported. If failures occur at 0.5% or 1%, or only for 98–100% coverage, the claim needs qualification. This experiment could be reduced if Experiment 1 already includes a sufficiently broad trigger and poison-rate sweep reported with confidence intervals.

To address subclaim 2, empirically characterize the actual AugMix and PixMix transformations using their public implementations on a public dataset such as CIFAR-10. Generate many augmented versions of the same images and measure whether the transformations are non-geometric pixel-level manipulations: estimate image alignment or optical-flow displacement to detect spatial warping, and separately measure pixel-intensity, color-histogram, frequency-spectrum, and texture-statistic changes. For AugMix, record the sampled operations, such as contrast, brightness, color, posterize, solarize, equalize, and related image-processing operations; for PixMix, record pixel-level mixing with auxiliary images or fractals. If most transformations preserve object geometry while altering color, intensity, texture, or pixel statistics, then PixMix and AugMix are valid examples for the claim. If substantial geometric transformations dominate, the claim’s categorization is inaccurate. This experiment may be unnecessary if the official AugMix and PixMix papers or code documentation are accepted as sufficient evidence that these methods primarily perform non-geometric pixel-level manipulations.
